title: New Workflow
author: Impetigocheez
selftext:
Over the last month and a half, I've completely changed my game development workflow, and it's honestly been a night-and-day difference.

I'm building a PSX-style tactical FPS inspired by games like Hell Let Loose, but designed as a single-player experience. It's still very much in the prototype stage, but for the first time I feel like I can actually see the finish line.

For the last six months I've been using Claude Code with Blender MCP, and I've finally reached the point where I really understand how to work with it instead of against it.

A few things that have made a huge difference:

\- Instead of asking it to make one-off assets, I build modular prop sets and then have it generate lots of variations.

\- I found a PSX character mesh/rig online and built a system where it creates U.S. soldiers, enemy soldiers, civilians, and multiple variants that are randomly assembled in-game, so every encounter feels a little different.

\- Villages are built from modular pieces with unique props, and NPCs follow schedules using in-game clocks and animations so the world feels alive.

\- The biggest breakthrough happened last night. Rather than paying for motion capture software, I added animation generation directly into my workflow. I feed it reference videos (or now I just tell it what to look for), and it creates Blender animations based on those references. Having a Mixamo animation library as a starting point helps it get surprisingly close, and since I'm aiming for a mid-2000s/PS2-style game instead of perfect AAA animation, the results have been more than good enough.

What's really crazy to me is that earlier this year I was making simple 2D games. It's not even the end of July, and now I'm building something that feels like a mid-2000s tactical FPS. I'm not trying to compete with modern AAA graphics—I just want to make fun, immersive games with solid gameplay.

I'm finally getting close to having something I can show publicly. The demo won't represent the full vision, but for the first time in a long time I'm genuinely excited about where this project is heading.

I'd love to hear if anyone else has found AI-assisted workflows that have dramatically sped up their indie development without sacrificing creativity.

replies.author: Cheedows
replies.body: Wow these look awesome. So the agent generated all thede guns etc? How did you get weapon grips to work?

replies.author: Impetigocheez
replies.body:
So to do this, it took a few weeks and reiterations of what I wanted

  
But like I was saying in other comments here. I found this rigging here: [https://comp3interactive.itch.io/low-poly-human-mesh](https://comp3interactive.itch.io/low-poly-human-mesh)

Than on chat gpt I got bitmap sheets for the faces and uniforms. here is an example of one of the sheets I got generated. Not everything is being used but its an option. 

I also made face atlas full of different US forces faces and made face atlas sheets specific to the Vietnamese people as well. 

Than with claudes help I attached the respective textures to the models in blender, I had to do manual editing of the UV WRAPS so if you don't know what that is, learn about those now to save yourself time. I've been learning blender on the side since feburary and am now finally feeling confident with it after all that time. So with claudes help I am super useful with Blender but even by myself im competent with it. 

Than for the guns, It has been an evovlving process because the NPCS in the game have been using the v1 gun models I got made but I have done like 6 to 10 different versions of some of these guns. I have about 15 in total and only 4 fully rigged up with the animations I really want. But thats part of getting better at doing this, you do 4 animation loops for different guns the last one you do will always look better than the first 3 so now i wanna go back and work on those guns before i keep moving forward cuz now i know what works and what doesn't work. 

But THE GUNS! I did a large batch coding session with the blender mcp about what I wanted. I made  a very detailed prompt and included small key features about each gun as well as asking for more research on the subject before modeling. And than in bout one or two prompts, where the follow up prompts are targeted clean ups of a few things here and there and me manually moving things around. But the guns are low poly, work from afar and dont need to be as detailed as a players hand held gun needs to be so I was able to make the npcs on both sides in about 3 to 4 days max.

replies.author: Impetigocheez
replies.body:
And to get the guns to grip properly, once I made the large batches you have claude add left and right hand node markers to each gun and youll have to audit them and fine tune it. Also add the muzzle markers to the ends of the guns so the bullets know where to come out of.

Than you apply the guns to the hands, and i had them all in resting idle aim pose so i could make that animation out of any of them work the best. Theres lots of small fine tuning but you just need paitence and again a vision of what you want to go for (im hitting that n64/PSX/Early PC Shooter look where the blockier but readable the better) but I would be lying if theres not times where I wanna rip my eyes out and punch claude in the face for some stuff that happens. That's why you should really be always trying to learn things on your own as well as having claude or any AI help you. 

  
That is the cognitive debt issue people are talking about for sure. I can envision lot more than I can technically do myself but thats also the beauty of what makes AI involved in these processes super cool.

replies.author: Impetigocheez
replies.body:
What specifics would you like to know?

I program inside Godot using Claude Code. I use blender mcp and godot mcp with Claude. I have a dedicated agent team called the War-Room that places any major request through a large debate and conversation with each game dev wing and there's a devils advocate as well. Thats how i run the long form requests or large refractors. 

For the blender aspect itself i found getting the psx rig and figuring out the best way to mesh it helped me feel confident to make different people quickly. My rigs also have a gib gore factor. I feed lots of examples of things and even sometimes still I have to get into the editor and make things look better but it really helps to have a specific graphical style in mind.

replies.author: Impetigocheez
replies.body: Also ive started running all my models at Medium effort and im getting way better outputs than full blast high effort. I think maybe make your plans with high effort but it eats the tokens too fast where this week I did all medium effort and my days off I was still able to get into my coding without having to pay for extra tokens

replies.author: NullzeroJP
replies.body:
I see, so you are mostly focused on the asset creation part now. 

Yeah, I haven’t found a good workflow for 3D gen yet. I know blender is an option, I just don’t know if LLMs have the spatial reasoning skills yet to get good results. 

Looking at the “toy” projects a lot of YouTube influencers generate… you know, like some fps shooter they try to one shot or some 3D platformer etc… these tests aren’t great as a measurement for how good it is to work with LLMs… but these “benchmarks” consistently show the same problems with their 3D generation. Namely: backward orientations, poor awareness of joint/hinge/pivot placement, and rotation animations.

Which is why I am hesitant to use an LLM for making 3D models. But I like your approach of hiding the blemishes and weak points with a psx aesthetic. It could work!
